# Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns

This document compresses the whole research folder into what you would
actually use in a design session: nineteen principles stated as prose, five
decision guides stated as questions, and a catalog of named anti-patterns
with their failure narratives. Nothing here is new; everything is justified
in the earlier documents.

A register note before the principles: everything in this document is
**doctrine** — deliberately imperative defaults distilled from documented S7
behavior and observed ecosystem practice, but laws of neither. The
imperative mood is a choice: a crisp default you can overrule for stated
reasons is more useful in a design session than a hedge you can ignore.
"Always" and "never" here mean "strong default," and when a principle
collides with a real constraint, the earlier documents carry the reasoning
needed to make the trade explicitly.

## Principles

**1. Model meaning before structure.** Begin with the domain's semantic atoms
— the indivisible meanings and their laws — and only then compose the
document structures that arrange them. Structure is the volatile part;
meaning is the stable contract. Systems (and dialects of a domain) that share
semantics can differ in structure and still interoperate; systems that share
only structure are totally coupled.

**2. Let construction be the proof.** Arrange the system so that no unlawful
object of a class can exist: boundary functions parse loose input into
objects or fail loudly, validators run on construction and every replacement,
and possession of the object certifies its laws. Downstream code demands
classes instead of re-checking contents.

**3. Constructors normalize; validators verify; boundaries translate.**
Coercion, canonicalization, and version gating happen once, at the boundary.
Validators judge canonical values only, and stay pure and cheap because they
run on every property write. A validator accommodating multiple input shapes
is a parser in the wrong place, running forever.

**4. Every invariant has one authoritative home.** Place each law on its
rung: external conformance at the wire, parsing at the boundary, type on the
property class, local law in the property validator, cross-property law in
the class validator, cross-object law in the aggregate root, operation
legality in the mutator, developer invariants in assertions. Each rung
assumes the rungs below and duplicates none. A cheap duplicate deliberately
retained for better boundary diagnostics is a documented trade; a law found
on two rungs *by accident* is a bug waiting to be two different laws.

**5. Invariants live at the lowest point that sees everything they mention.**
A channel range belongs to the channel property; a start-before-end rule to
the class; unique-ids-across-the-collection to the root that holds the
collection. Placing a law lower than its visibility horizon makes it
uncheckable; higher, and it runs too often and knows too much.

**6. Presence is a four-way decision.** Required-at-construction, nullable in
the model, defaulted, and omitted-on-serialization are independent axes, and
JSON's omitted / null / empty forms are distinct meanings. Decide per
property, record the policy, and never let one `optional` flag conflate what
"the user cleared this" and "the user never touched this."

**7. Constants are identity, not state.** If two instances of a class can
never differ on a field, the field is part of what the class *is*: model it
as a computed property or inject it at serialization, and keep it out of the
constructor. Store it only when round-trip fidelity or spec evolution demands
that instances carry it.

**8. Represent alternatives as alternatives.** Flag fields, mutually
exclusive nullables, and mode strings are sum types flattened into products.
Give variants honest representation: subclass families when fields or
behavior differ, enum properties when only the tag differs, unions for
primitive alternatives in one slot. Recover exhaustiveness with loud
defaults and registry-driven tests.

**9. Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure.**
Parents contribute a property schema and a dispatch position to things that
genuinely are the parent. Everything else — nesting, reuse, independent
dimensions — is composition. Hierarchies stay shallow: abstract root,
concrete leaves, intermediate levels only when they add both schema and a
dispatch target. Inherit from a base type only when the object *is* that
primitive.

**10. Behavior belongs to generics, and interfaces are generic-sets plus
laws.** Design the verb vocabulary as deliberately as the class graph. An
extension point is a set of generics an implementor must support *and* the
laws those methods must satisfy — write the laws down, executably where
possible. Reach for multiple dispatch when behavior genuinely varies along
two type axes; it turns a conditionals matrix into small methods.

**11. Values in the core, references in the shell.** Records of fact are
immutable S7 values transformed by pure functions; ongoing processes with
identity — sessions, caches, conversations — are R6 or environments at the
system's rim. The domain must be reconstructible from the values alone.

**12. Mutate atomically, through the front door.** Invariants spanning
several properties imply every update of those properties goes through one
atomic replacement (`S7::set_props()`), wrapped in a mutator function so
callers cannot do it wrong. Guarantees hold for clients of the exported
surface; make the front door the easiest path.

**13. One canonical artifact, many projections.** When several outputs encode
the same knowledge — an expression and a legend; a class graph and its
documentation; a wire format and a pretty printer — designate one canonical
source (usually a small, reviewable data structure) and generate every
projection. Hand-maintained parallel encodings *will* diverge.

**14. Property access is cheap and pure.** Getters compute derivations; they
never perform I/O, never mutate, never surprise. The moment `x@thing` can be
slow or effectful, the object stops being data in the reader's mind, and the
whole value-semantics reasoning collapses.

**15. Abstractions must earn their keep.** Every layer of indirection pays
rent by absorbing a demonstrated axis of variation — behavioral variation
across types, meaning shared across sites, representation churn at a
boundary. Abstract after the third occurrence, not the first. Delete layers
that no longer pay. The ecosystem's convergent evolution (independent
projects growing the same enum/scalar/presence property helpers) is the
positive form of this evidence: those particular abstractions keep earning.

**16. Schemas are contracts and inputs, not blueprints.** Validate against
external schemas with the schema ecosystem's own tools at the wire; read
schemas as a census that informs hand-designed models; generate tables (enums,
name maps, requiredness) rather than class graphs. A 1:1 mirror of an
external type system imports its structure and discards the chance to encode
meaning. And when your own model is the source of truth, store its
constraints as data so the schema can be *projected* from it — one datum, and
the validator and the published contract cannot disagree.

**17. Refuse to guess.** Where no correct behavior is known, an error beats a
default. sqlr states the reason perfectly in declining to ship an "ANSI SQL"
fallback dialect: an untestable default "would quietly accumulate behaviour no
database had ever accepted." The same logic condemns silent coercion of
ambiguous input, fallback branches for "unknown type," and any code path no
test can exercise against a real authority. A loud, early error is
information; a guess is deferred corruption.

**18. Check as early as the inputs allow, as late as the context requires.**
The value of a check is proportional to the cost of the work it gates.
Declarations should validate themselves at package load (a default violating
its own bounds is the author's bug, catchable before any user exists);
configurations should validate fully before the expensive run they configure;
and laws that mention context not yet in hand — data dimensions, live
resources — should be *declared* at construction and *checked* in one named
pass at the moment the context arrives, never guessed at and never skipped.

**19. Failure travels one of two channels; choose per boundary.** Conditions
(classed, chained, `cli`-formatted) are the channel for bugs and contract
violations — control flow that should stop. Result-style values are the
channel when failure is an expected outcome the caller branches on as data —
partial batches, fallible lookups feeding pipelines. Convert between the
channels at one designed adapter (resultr's `wrap_in_result()` is the model),
never with ad hoc `tryCatch` scattered through the core.

## Decision guides

Formulated as the questions to ask, in order, rather than flowcharts to
follow mechanically.

**Which object system?** Is it fundamentally a homogeneous vector that must
slice and live in data frames? — vctrs. Does it have identity and a lifetime,
with observers sharing its changes? — R6 or an environment. Is it a domain
value with laws and dispatchable behavior? — S7. Is it a veneer for ecosystem
politeness? — S3. Mixed answers mean a hybrid, which is normal.

**Which sum-type encoding?** Do variants differ in fields, or does behavior
dispatch on them? — subclass family under an abstract parent. Do they differ
only in the tag? — enum-valued property. Is it several primitive shapes
lawful in one slot? — union. Is the wire genuinely one bag with conditional
fields, variants are many and trivial, and dispatch is never needed? — a
discriminator plus class validator, chosen consciously as denormalization.

**Which semantic-type tier?** Does the concept merely repeat a validation
shape across sites? — a reused property definition. Must it be impossible to
confuse with its base primitive, or does dispatch need it, while it remains
truly a primitive? — a class inheriting the base type. Does it have parts, or
operations of its own? — a composite class.

**Stored field, identity, or boundary-normalized?** Can two instances of the
class differ on it? If no — identity (computed property or
serializer-injected). If yes — must round-trips preserve the caller's exact
value? If yes — stored, with lenient parsing at the boundary and one
canonical stored form. Might the spec extend the value set? — stored enum
with a parse-time version gate.

**How deep should an embedded language go?** Does anything analyze or
transform the expressions, or target more than one output format? If no —
opaque passthrough, with the engine's validator as judge. Do humans
hand-write the expressions painfully? — constructor combinators (shallow
embedding). Is analysis, optimization, or multi-target translation the
product? — typed AST with generic passes (deep embedding). Representation as
deep as the analysis, and no deeper.

## Anti-pattern catalog

Named, so design reviews can point at them.

**Schema cosplay.** Mirroring an external type system one class per
interface. The model inherits every serialization quirk as a nominal type,
class count tracks the schema forever, and no semantic layer exists because
the schema never had one. *Tell:* classes whose names and nesting match the
wire exactly, none of which ever gains a method.

**Validator soup.** The same law encoded in the constructor, the property
validator, the class validator, and a boundary schema. The encodings drift;
error messages disagree; nobody knows which one fired. *Tell:* fixing one
validation bug requires a grep.

**Shotgun parsing.** Input checks interleaved with processing across many
functions, no single point after which input is known-good, rejection
possible after side effects. *Tell:* `is.null()` and `is.character()` guards
deep in core logic; functions that "defensively" re-check their own
package's objects.

**Boolean blindness.** Check functions returning `TRUE`/`FALSE` whose
callers immediately need the *why* or the *what* — so they re-derive it.
*Tell:* `if (is_valid(x)) { ... }` followed by code that re-inspects `x` for
the very facts validity established. Return parsed evidence, not verdicts.

**The God validator.** One class validator enforcing property-local rules,
cross-property rules, and collection rules in a hundred lines. Placement
discipline lost; every rung's law in one place, none assumable by the others.
*Tell:* a class validator that re-checks types.

**Convert-everything.** Routing lossy, contextual, one-to-many translation
through a coercion generic because it exists. Coercion generics
(`convert(from, to)`) suit faithful pairwise conversion; translation with
diagnostics, options, and asset generation deserves named functions with
room for a context argument and a report. *Tell:* a `convert` method with
side effects or a dozen options.

**Expression-system envy.** Re-implementing an engine's expression type
system in property validators — badly, partially, and forever chasing the
spec. The engine's validator owns rung 0. *Tell:* a validator that walks
nested lists interpreting operator names.

**Decorative hierarchy.** Inheritance introduced to share field names or to
"organize" classes that never dispatch differently. Dispatch will eventually
take the fake is-a seriously. *Tell:* an abstract parent with one child, or
parents whose children never appear in a method signature.

**The mutable domain object.** Domain facts held in R6 "for convenience,"
surrendering local reasoning, cheap snapshots, and testability to avoid
reassignment. *Tell:* `$clone()` calls sprinkled defensively; tests full of
setup/teardown for what should be a value.

**Nullable confusion.** `NULL` doing triple duty as "required but not yet
supplied," "explicitly cleared," and "omitted on the wire," with no presence
policy. *Tell:* code that cannot distinguish an untouched field from a
cleared one; serializers with ad-hoc per-field `if (!is.null())` decisions.

**Premature DSL.** Combinators, quotation, and clever printing built before
any user wrote the target structures by hand long enough to reveal which
constructions are actually painful. The DSL then ossifies the wrong
abstractions. *Tell:* a DSL whose vocabulary mirrors the wire format
one-to-one instead of the domain's own idioms.

**Effectful getter.** A property that reads a file, calls an API, or mutates
a cache. Data access becomes action at a distance; cost and effects become
invisible at every `@`. *Tell:* property access inside a loop dominating a
profile; getters needing error handling.

**Boundary leakage.** Wire names, omit-empty decisions, or dialect quirks
appearing in core logic instead of the one serializer pair. *Tell:*
`"source-layer"` (the wire spelling) as a string anywhere except
`to_wire()`/`from_wire()`.

## A closing note on judgment

The principles compress experience, but they trade against each other in real
designs: parse-don't-validate argues for strictness at the boundary while
round-trip fidelity argues for permissive pass-through nodes; earned
abstraction argues for waiting while semantic atoms argue for naming meanings
early; shallow hierarchies argue against intermediate classes while shared
schema sometimes argues for them. The earlier documents exist so that when
two principles collide, the *reasons* behind each are available and the
trade can be made explicitly, on the record, instead of by whichever slogan
was remembered first.
